pages.text: Say £100 grows 100% over a year. Paid as one part at the year's end, it doubles to £200. Now pay it in two halves of 50%. The first half takes £100 to £150. The second half's 50% is taken of £150, not £100, so it adds £75 and ends at £225. Splitting helps because each part's growth starts earning straight away.

pages.task: Now pay the year's 100% as four quarters of 25%. Each quarter's 25% is taken of the pot by then. What is the pot at the year's end?
pages.why: Each quarter multiplies the pot by `1 + 1/4 = 1.25`, so the year gives `100 × 1.25⁴` ≈ £244.14. The rises grow, from £25 at first to £48.83 at the end, because each one is 25% of a bigger pot.

pages.alt: A graph, time along the bottom and pounds up the side. A smooth curve behind. A staircase of 365 parts a year. £271.46. A slider for the parts the year is split into, at 365 parts. The year's totals so far: 1 part, 2; 2 parts, 2.25; 4 parts, 2.4414; 12 parts, 2.6130; 365 parts, 2.7146. On a line they crowd towards e, about 2.718.
pages.name: More and more parts
pages.text: Split the year into `n` equal parts: each multiplies the pot by `1 + 1/n`, so the year multiplies it by `(1 + 1/n)ⁿ`. More parts make smaller steps that hug the smooth curve, and the total grows by less each time, settling near 2.718. That fixed number is called [[e]], about 2.71828, a constant like π, not a letter you choose. Slide the number of parts.

pages.name: Every hour
pages.task: A year has 8,760 hours. Guess before you step there. What does £100 reach when its 100% is paid in 8,760 parts?
pages.why: Going from 365 parts to 8,760 adds only about 35p, from £271.46 to £271.81. Each extra split adds interest on ever smaller slices of interest, so the total settles. The year's total, 2.7181, is now close to e, about 2.71828.

pages.text: Growth that never pauses is the smooth curve the staircases hug. At 100% a year it makes the pot e times bigger each year, so after `t` years it is `eᵗ` times the start, worked on the calculator's eˣ key. Part of a year works too: two half-years make a year, so each half multiplies the pot by `e^0.5`, the number that times itself gives e. That is about 1.6487, so £100 becomes about £164.87. Two years give `e² ≈ 7.389`.

pages.alt: A graph, time along the bottom and pounds up the side. A smooth curve. £100. A smooth curve. £738.91.
pages.name: Two years
pages.task: £100 grows 100% a year, never pausing. What is it after 2 years?
pages.why: Each year multiplies the pot by e, so 2 years multiply it by `e × e = e²` ≈ 7.389. That makes `100 × e²` ≈ £738.91.

pages.text: A smaller rate works the same way. 5% a year in 100 parts adds 0.05% a part, as 100% in 2,000 parts does, so a year at 5% is 100 of those 2,000 parts, a twentieth of a year at 100%: `e^(1/20) = e^0.05 ≈ 1.0513`. And `t` years at 5% are `t/20` years at 100%, `e^(0.05t)`. At any [[growth rate]] `k`, as a decimal, the power is the rate times the time. Slide it to 100%, where the 1-part bar stops at little more than half the never-pausing one.

pages.task: At 5% a year, never pausing, a pot is `e^(0.05t)` times the start after `t` years. What does each year multiply it by?
pages.why: One year puts `t = 1` in the power, so each year multiplies the pot by `e^0.05 ≈ 1.0513`. The rate, 0.05, is not the factor. And 1.0513 is a little more than the 1.05 that paying once gives, because the growth earns as it goes.

pages.task: A capacitor's voltage is `400 e^(−0.1t)` volts, `t` seconds after it starts to fall. What is it after 10 seconds?
pages.why: The power is `−0.1 × 10 = −1`, and `e^(−1) ≈ 0.368`. So the voltage is `400 × e^(−1)` ≈ 147 V, a little over a third of the start.

pages.task: A pot grows 10% a year for 3 years, never pausing. What is it multiplied by?
pages.why: Multiply the rate by the time, `0.1 × 3 = 0.3`, and press eˣ to get `e^0.3 ≈ 1.35`. That is just above `1.1³ = 1.331`, paid once a year, which is above `1 + 3 × 0.1 = 1.3`, adding 10% of the start three times.

pages.task: £1,000 grows at 6% a year, never pausing. What is it worth after one year?
pages.why: The rate times the time is `0.06 × 1 = 0.06`, so it reaches `1,000 × e^0.06` ≈ £1,061.84. Paid monthly it would be `1,000 × 1.005¹²` ≈ £1,061.68, and paid once £1,060. At a small rate, never pausing adds only a little.

pages.text: One look ahead, for later. Here is `eˣ` on the slope tracker you met before. At every point its slope equals its height; here you can check it from `x = 0` to `x = 2`, 1 at `x = 0` and about 2.718 at `x = 1`. That is growth whose rate is proportional to its current value. Later work on derivatives takes it further, and nothing here depends on it.
